questions.question: The Tapti River originates from which mountain range?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Satpura Range**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Tapti River originates from **Multai**, located in the **Satpura Range** of Madhya Pradesh, India.
 
• The Tapti River flows westward, one of the few rivers in peninsular India to do so, and drains into the **Arabian Sea**.
 
• It is approximately **724 km long**, making it one of the major rivers of central India.
 
• The Tapti River passes through three states: **Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra,** and **Gujarat**.
 
• The river is known for supporting agricultural activities in its basin, which covers a total area of around **65,145 square kilometers**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Satpura Range:**

 
 
• The Satpura Range is a hill range in central India, stretching across Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.
 
• The range is a part of the **Deccan Plateau** and is known for its rich biodiversity and dense forests.
 
• Prominent peaks in the Satpura Range include Dhupgarh (the highest point in Madhya Pradesh) and Pachmarhi.
 
• It is an important source of rivers such as the Tapti, Narmada, and Godavari.
 
 
 
• **Westward Flowing Rivers in India:**
 
 
• Most rivers in India flow eastward towards the Bay of Bengal; however, a few like the Tapti, Narmada, and Mahi flow westward.
 
• These rivers drain into the Arabian Sea, contributing significantly to the western coastal ecosystem.
 
 
 
• **Arabian Sea Drainage System:**
 
 
• The Tapti River forms part of the Arabian Sea drainage system along with other westward flowing rivers.
 
• These rivers often carve narrow valleys and are important for irrigation and hydroelectric projects.
 
 
 
• **Multai:**
 
 
• Multai is a town in Madhya Pradesh known as the origin point of the Tapti River.
 
• The name "Tapti" is derived from the goddess Tapti, worshipped in Hindu mythology.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Find and Replace feature (Ctrl + H) in MS Word 2019?

options.text: To change the font of the selected text
To search for specific text and replace it with other text

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To search for specific text and replace it with other text**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Find and Replace** feature in MS Word 2019 is used to **locate specific text or phrases** within a document and replace them with alternative text if required.
 
• It is accessed using the keyboard shortcut **Ctrl + H** or through the "Home" tab in the "Editing" group.
 
• This feature enables users to make **bulk changes** in a document efficiently, saving time and effort for repetitive edits.
 
• Advanced options in "Find and Replace" allow users to search for text with specific formatting, such as bold, italic, or specific fonts, and replace it with similar or modified formatting.
 
• It helps in maintaining consistency across large documents by ensuring uniform corrections or modifications.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Search Options in Find and Replace:**

 
 
• Users can perform **case-sensitive searches** by enabling the "Match Case" option.
 
• The "Find Whole Words Only" option ensures only complete words matching the search term are located.
 
• Wildcard characters can be used to perform advanced and flexible searches.
 
 
 
• **Go To Feature:**
 
 
• The "Go To" tab within the Find and Replace dialog box allows users to navigate to specific pages, sections, or line numbers in a document.
 
 
 
• **Formatting Search:**
 
 
• Users can search for text with specific formatting attributes, such as font size, color, or paragraph settings, using the "Format" option in the dialog box.
 
 
 
• **Limitations:**
 
 
• The feature does not support searching for non-text elements such as images or tables directly.
 
• Complex edits may require manual intervention despite using the Replace function.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Ideal for editing large documents, such as legal contracts, research papers, or reports, where repetitive terms or formatting need adjustment.

questions.question: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent extremist leader, wrote the newspaper 'Mahratta' in which language?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**English**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, a key leader of the Indian independence movement, was a staunch nationalist and one of the pioneers of the extremist faction.
 
• Tilak edited two newspapers: **'Kesari'**, published in Marathi, and **'Mahratta'**, published in English.
 
• The newspaper **'Mahratta'** was founded to promote nationalism and disseminate Tilak's political ideologies among educated Indians.
 
• Through his writings in 'Mahratta', Tilak criticized British policies and advocated for Swaraj (self-rule).
 
• The English-language newspaper was instrumental in reaching a wider audience, including educated Indians and intellectuals across the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:**

 
 
• He was popularly known as **'Lokmanya Tilak'**, meaning 'accepted by the people as their leader.'
 
• He is regarded as the 'Father of Indian Unrest' due to his strong opposition to British rule.
 
• Tilak was one of the first leaders to demand complete independence (Purna Swaraj) for India.
 
• His famous slogan was **"Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it."**
 
 
 
• **'Kesari' and 'Mahratta' Newspapers:**
 
 
• 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English) were used as platforms to spread anti-colonial sentiments.
 
• 'Kesari' was especially influential among the Marathi-speaking population.
 
• Both newspapers played a crucial role in inspiring Indians to fight for independence.
 
 
 
• **Concept of Swaraj:**
 
 
• Swaraj, meaning self-rule, was a central theme of Tilak's political philosophy.
 
• Tilak believed in empowering Indians politically, culturally, and economically to achieve independence.
 
• His ideas laid the foundation for future leaders like Mahatma Gandhi in the struggle for freedom.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak remains one of the most respected and influential leaders of India’s freedom struggle.
 
• His contributions continue to be studied and celebrated in Indian political and historical discourse.

questions.question: India Infoline Finance Limited (IIFL Finance), India’s leading non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), has rebranded how many of its existing branches as all-women staffed ‘Shakti’ branches to mark Women’s Day (8 March 2025)?

questions.question: Following the provisions of the 74th Constitutional Amendment, 1992, which of the following terms is used for urban governance in areas transitioning from rural to urban?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagar Panchayats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• es Nagar Panchayats are urban local bodiestablished under the provisions of the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
 
• They are constituted for areas transitioning from rural to urban due to population growth or other factors of urbanization.
 
• The primary purpose of Nagar Panchayats is to manage urban governance in these transitional areas while ensuring smooth administrative operations.
 
• As per the Constitution, Nagar Panchayats are recognized as one of the three types of municipal entities: Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• Nagar Panchayats consist of elected representatives and function under the control of the state government, addressing urban planning, development, and basic infrastructure needs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**

 
 
• This amendment introduced the concept of urban local bodies, including Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• It provided constitutional recognition to local governance and decentralized decision-making in urban areas.
 
• The act aimed at empowering urban local bodies to function as institutions of self-government under Article 243Q.
 
 
 
• **Urbanization in India**
 
 
• India's urban population is steadily growing due to migration, industrialization, and expansion of economic opportunities.
 
• Transitional areas often require structured urban governance to address challenges like housing, sanitation, and infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Nagar Panchayats and Rural Bodies**
 
 
• While rural bodies like Gram Panchayats cater to villages, Nagar Panchayats focus on urban governance in transitioning areas.
 
• Nagar Panchayats deal with urban challenges such as traffic management, waste disposal, and urban planning.
 
 
 
• **Role of State Governments**
 
 
• State governments play a crucial role in defining the criteria for establishing Nagar Panchayats.
 
• They provide funds, guidance, and administrative support to enable effective urban governance.

questions.question: What major power did the 74th Amendment Act, 1992, provide to Urban Local Bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Constitutional outline for governance**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 74th Amendment Act, 1992, provided a **constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**, ensuring their governance framework under the Indian Constitution.
 
• The amendment added **Part IX-A** (The Municipalities) to the Constitution, detailing the structure, composition, and functions of ULBs.
 
• It mandated the creation of three types of municipalities: **Nagar Panchayats**, **Municipal Councils**, and **Municipal Corporations**, based on population size.
 
• It introduced the concept of **decentralized governance**, empowering ULBs to plan and implement development programs and manage local resources effectively.
 
• The act also provided for the establishment of a **State Finance Commission (SFC)** to allocate financial resources to these bodies, ensuring fiscal autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part IX-A of the Constitution:**

 
 
• Introduced by the 74th Amendment, it provides a **constitutional framework for urban governance**.
 
• It includes Articles 243P to 243ZG, outlining the composition, powers, and responsibilities of municipalities.
 
 
 
• **State Finance Commission (SFC):**
 
 
• Established under Article 243-I, it ensures **equitable distribution of financial resources** between the state government and ULBs.
 
• The SFC reviews financial positions of ULBs and recommends measures for their fiscal sustainability.
 
 
 
• **District Planning Committees (DPCs):**
 
 
• Mandated under Article 243ZD, DPCs integrate plans prepared by Panchayats and Municipalities into a cohesive **district development plan**.
 
 
 
• **Empowered Municipalities:**
 
 
• The 12th Schedule of the Constitution lists **18 functional areas** for ULBs, including urban planning, water supply, sanitation, and public health.
 
• This ensures enhanced autonomy and accountability in addressing local governance issues.

questions.question: When appointing judges to the High Courts, the President of India is required to consult which officials apart from the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the respective State?

options.text: The members of the State Legislature

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The State Governor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under Article 217 of the Indian Constitution, the President is required to consult the Chief Justice of India, the Chief Justice of the respective High Court, and the **Governor of the concerned State** before appointing judges to the High Courts.
 
• The role of the State Governor in this process is advisory, and the final decision is made by the President.
 
• The consultation process ensures the appointment of qualified and unbiased individuals to the judiciary, maintaining the integrity of the judicial system.
 
• The Chief Justice of India plays a critical role in providing recommendations to the President based on merit and judicial expertise.
 
• This constitutional provision is designed to promote a collaborative process involving key stakeholders in the judiciary and executive.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 217 of the Constitution of India:**

 
 
• It deals with the appointment and conditions of service of High Court judges.
 
• The President appoints judges after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the concerned state, and sometimes other judges as deemed necessary.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Chief Justice of India:**
 
 
• The Chief Justice of India provides recommendations to the President, ensuring judicial appointments are based on merit and integrity.
 
• This role is crucial for maintaining the independence of the judiciary.
 
 
 
• **High Court Judges:**
 
 
• They are responsible for adjudicating cases and upholding the Constitution within their respective jurisdictions.
 
• High Court judges hold office until the age of 62.
 
 
 
• **Governor's Advisory Role:**
 
 
• The Governor of the state provides input during the consultation process, representing the state’s interests.
 
• While the Governor’s role is advisory, the President has the final say in judicial appointments.

questions.question: In one of his famous works, Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi claims that the founder of the _____ was a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sayyid Dynasty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sayyid Dynasty ruled Delhi Sultanate from **1414 to 1451 CE** after the fall of the Tughlaq Dynasty.
 
• The founder of the dynasty, **Khizr Khan**, claimed to be a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad through his lineage.
 
• Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi, a chronicler of the era, documented the claim of Khizr Khan's **prophetic descent** in his historical works.
 
• The Sayyids were known for their relatively weak control over the Delhi Sultanate and faced constant challenges from regional rulers.
 
• The dynasty ended when **Bahlul Lodi** established the Lodi Dynasty in 1451 CE, marking the end of the Sayyid rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Delhi Sultanate:**

 
 
• The Delhi Sultanate was a series of Islamic dynasties that ruled over India from 1206 to 1526 CE.
 
• It consisted of five dynasties: Slave Dynasty, Khilji Dynasty, Tughlaq Dynasty, Sayyid Dynasty, and Lodi Dynasty.
 
• The Sultanate played a significant role in the cultural and architectural development of India, introducing Persian art and Islamic architecture.
 
 
 
• **Khizr Khan:**
 
 
• Khizr Khan was the founder of the Sayyid Dynasty and ruled from 1414 to 1421 CE.
 
• He was appointed as the governor of Multan by Timur before ascending to power in Delhi.
 
• Khizr Khan did not assume the title of Sultan but ruled as a vassal of the Timurid Empire.
 
 
 
• **Yahya bin Ahmad Sirhindi:**
 
 
• He was a historian during the Sayyid period and authored the **Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi**, which chronicles the history of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• His works provide valuable insights into the political, social, and cultural aspects of the era.
 
 
 
• **Timur’s Invasion of Delhi:**
 
 
• Timur invaded Delhi in 1398 CE, leading to massive destruction and weakening the Tughlaq Dynasty.
 
• This invasion set the stage for the rise of the Sayyid Dynasty, which emerged as Timur’s vassal rulers in Delhi.

questions.question: Who among the following was awarded the Ramsar Award for 'Wetland Wise Use' in March 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jayashree Vencatesan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Jayashree Vencatesan was awarded the Ramsar Award for "Wetland Wise Use" in March 2025 for her significant contributions to wetland conservation and sustainable management.
 
• The Ramsar Award recognizes individuals, organizations, and governments for exceptional efforts in the conservation and wise use of wetlands.
 
• Jayashree Vencatesan is a renowned environmentalist and the managing trustee of Care Earth Trust, an organization working on biodiversity conservation.
 
• Her work includes promoting community-based wetland management and advocating for policies that ensure the ecological and socio-economic sustainability of wetlands.
 
• The Ramsar Award is one of the most prestigious global recognitions in the field of wetland conservation, presented by the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ramsar Convention:**

 
 
• It is an international treaty adopted in 1971 in Ramsar, Iran, aimed at conserving wetlands and promoting their sustainable use.
 
• The convention designates specific wetlands as "Ramsar Sites" for their ecological significance.
 
• Wetlands play a crucial role in biodiversity conservation, water purification, flood control, and climate regulation.
 
 
 
• **Wetland Wise Use:**
 
 
• Wise use refers to the sustainable utilization of wetlands to maintain their ecological character.
 
• It ensures that wetland resources are used in a way that benefits both biodiversity and local communities.
 
 
 
• **India and Ramsar Sites:**
 
 
• India is home to over 75 Ramsar Sites, making it one of the countries with the highest number of wetlands designated under the Ramsar Convention.
 
• These sites include Sundarbans, Chilika Lake, and Keoladeo National Park, among others.
 
 
 
• **Care Earth Trust:**
 
 
• Care Earth Trust is a Chennai-based NGO focused on biodiversity conservation and ecosystem management.
 
• It works extensively on wetland restoration, urban biodiversity, and climate change mitigation strategies.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT allowed under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dual citizenship**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Citizenship Act, 1955 governs the acquisition, determination, and termination of Indian citizenship.
 
• India does not allow **dual citizenship**. A citizen of India cannot hold citizenship of another country simultaneously.
 
• The Act provides for citizenship through five modes: **birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory**.
 
• Dual citizenship is not permitted because India follows a policy of single citizenship, ensuring uniform national identity and allegiance.
 
• Indian citizens acquiring foreign citizenship must renounce their Indian citizenship as per the provisions of the Act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Naturalization:**

 
 
• Naturalization is a mode of acquiring citizenship for foreign nationals who fulfill eligibility criteria like residence in India for a specified period and good character.
 
• Applicants must renounce their citizenship of another country to become Indian citizens.
 
 
 
• **Descent-based Citizenship:**
 
 
• A person born outside India is considered an Indian citizen by descent if either of their parents is an Indian citizen.
 
• Specific conditions apply based on the date of birth and registration requirements under the Citizenship Act, 1955.
 
 
 
• **Registration:**
 
 
• Citizenship through registration is available for individuals like persons of Indian origin or spouses of Indian citizens who meet prescribed conditions.
 
• They must reside in India for a specific period before applying for registration.
 
 
 
• **Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI):**
 
 
• Though dual citizenship is not allowed, the government offers the **OCI scheme** for people of Indian origin who are citizens of other countries.
 
• OCI status provides several rights but does not equate to full citizenship, such as voting rights or eligibility for government jobs.
 
 
 
• **Renunciation and Termination of Citizenship:**
 
 
• Citizenship can be renounced voluntarily by individuals or terminated by the government in case of fraud or disloyalty.
 
• The Act specifies detailed procedures for renunciation and termination to ensure compliance with legal frameworks.

questions.question: In India, judicial review is considered as:

options.text: The power of the judiciary to pronounce upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders
the power of the judiciary to question the wisdom of the executive orders after they are passed by the Union cabinet
the power of the judiciary to review all the legislative enactments before they are assented to by the President
the power of the judiciary to question the wisdom of the laws enacted by the legislatures

questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** the power of the judiciary to pronounce upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders**__**.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Judicial review in India is a power granted to the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative acts and executive orders.
 
• This principle ensures that laws and executive actions do not violate the provisions of the Constitution of India.
 
• The concept is derived from Article 13, which states that any law inconsistent with the Constitution shall be void.
 
• Judicial review in India encompasses reviewing administrative decisions, legislative enactments, and constitutional amendments.
 
• It acts as a crucial mechanism for maintaining the supremacy of the Constitution and protecting fundamental rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review**

 
 
• Judicial review originated in the United States through the landmark case of **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
 
• It ensures checks and balances among the three organs of the government: executive, legislature, and judiciary.
 
• In India, judicial review is limited compared to the United States but is pivotal in safeguarding constitutional democracy.
 
 
 
• **Articles Related to Judicial Review in India**
 
 
• **Article 13:** Declares that laws inconsistent with or in derogation of fundamental rights are void.
 
• **Article 32:** Provides the right to constitutional remedies, allowing citizens to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of rights.
 
• **Article 226:** Empowers High Courts to issue orders or writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and other purposes.
 
 
 
• **Types of Judicial Review**
 
 
• **Review of Legislative Actions:** Ensures that laws passed by the legislature adhere to constitutional provisions.
 
• **Review of Executive Actions:** Examines the validity of decisions made by the executive branch.
 
• **Review of Constitutional Amendments:** Determines whether amendments violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Basic Structure Doctrine**
 
 
• This doctrine was established in the landmark **Keshavananda Bharati Case (1973)**.
 
• The judiciary can strike down constitutional amendments if they violate the essential features of the Constitution.
 
• Examples of basic structure elements include the supremacy of the Constitution, secularism, and judicial independence.

questions.question: Post 1991 economic reforms, India witnessed significant changes in the banking sector. What is one major reform introduced in the banking sector?

__
 
• **Deregulation of interest rates **was a key reform introduced in the Indian banking sector as part of the **post-1991 economic reforms**.
 
• Prior to this, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) tightly regulated interest rates, but deregulation allowed banks to determine interest rates based on market conditions.
 
• This reform enhanced competition among banks, resulting in better services and improved financial efficiency.
 
• LiberalCreation approved financials to meet diverse customer demands to compete on deposits and loans
 
• It aimed to develop a more flexible and market-driven banking system, which was crucial for India's transition to a more liberalized economy.

• **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR):**

 
 
• SLR is the percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that must be maintained in liquid assets like cash, gold, or government-approved securities before providing credit to customers.
 
• It is used by the RBI to control inflation and regulate the credit flow in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate:**
 
 
• The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks, while the reverse repo rate is the rate at which RBI borrows money from banks.
 
• These tools are used to control liquidity and inflation in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Banking Sector Liberalization:**
 
 
• Reforms after 1991 allowed the entry of private and foreign banks into India, leading to growth and innovation in services.
 
• This also led to significant investments in technology, improving efficiency and customer experience.
 
 
 
• **Non-Performing Assets (NPAs):**
 
 
• NPAs are loans or advances where the borrower has stopped making interest or principal repayments for a specified period.
 
• The banking reforms also aimed to address the issue of rising NPAs through better credit risk management and recovery mechanisms.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms exhibits both autotrophic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Euglena**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Euglena** is a unique single-celled organism that exhibits both autotrophic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition.
 
• In the presence of sunlight, Euglena performs **photosynthesis** using chlorophyll, making it autotrophic.
 
• In the absence of sunlight, Euglena can obtain nutrition heterotrophically by **absorbing organic matter** from its environment.
 
• Euglena belongs to the kingdom **Protista** and is often studied as an example of a mixotrophic organism.
 
• This dual nutritional capability enables Euglena to survive in a variety of habitats, making it highly adaptable.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Autotrophic Nutrition:**

 
 
• It refers to the mode of nutrition where organisms synthesize their own food using simple inorganic substances like carbon dioxide and water.
 
• Photosynthesis, using sunlight, is the most common method of autotrophic nutrition.
 
• Examples include plants, algae, and some bacteria.
 
 
 
• **Heterotrophic Nutrition:**
 
 
• In this mode, organisms depend on other organisms for food.
 
• Heterotrophs are unable to synthesize their own food and rely on consuming organic matter.
 
• Examples include animals, fungi, and certain protists like Amoeba.
 
 
 
• **Mixotrophic Nutrition:**
 
 
• Organisms like Euglena that can switch between autotrophic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition exhibit mixotrophic nutrition.
 
• This ability provides flexibility and survival advantages in fluctuating environmental conditions.
 
 
 
• **Kingdom Protista:**
 
 
• It includes a diverse group of eukaryotic organisms that are primarily unicellular.
 
• Protists can be autotrophic, heterotrophic, or mixotrophic.
 
• Examples include Euglena, Amoeba, and Paramecium.

questions.question: Which Act transferred the power of governance from the East India Company to the British Crown?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1858**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1858** marked the end of the East India Company’s rule and transferred the administration of India directly to the British Crown.
 
• The act established the position of a **Secretary of State for India**, who was responsible for overseeing Indian affairs in Britain.
 
• It introduced the **Council of India** to assist the Secretary of State, comprising 15 members, mainly former directors of the East India Company.
 
• This act formally ended the dual governance system and centralized power under the British government, following the failure of the East India Company during the **1857 Revolt**.
 
• The Governor-General of India was renamed as **Viceroy of India**, representing the Crown directly in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charter Act, 1833**

 
 
• This act centralized legislative powers in India by establishing a single legislative council for all British territories in India.
 
• It marked the end of the East India Company's trading rights and made it an administrative body.
 
• It introduced the idea of an open competition for civil services, but the provision was not implemented until later.
 
 
 
• **Regulating Act, 1773**
 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British government to regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.
 
• It established a Governor-General in Bengal and created a Supreme Court at Fort William, Kolkata.
 
• The act aimed to curb corruption and mismanagement but had limited success.
 
 
 
• **Pitt's India Act, 1784**
 
 
• This act introduced the concept of dual control between the British government and the East India Company.
 
• It created a Board of Control to supervise civil, military, and revenue administration in India.
 
• The act aimed to address issues of governance after the shortcomings of the Regulating Act.
 
 
 
• **Indian Rebellion of 1857**
 
 
• The widespread uprising against British rule revealed the flaws in the East India Company's administrative structure.
 
• It directly led to the implementation of the Government of India Act, 1858, which centralized power under the Crown.
 
• The rebellion is considered one of the most significant events in Indian history, leading to the dissolution of the East India Company.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the shape of a sinusoidal wave signal during one complete cycle?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**S-shaped wave**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A sinusoidal wave signal completes one cycle in a characteristic smooth, oscillatory motion resembling an **S-shaped curve**.
 
• Sinusoidal waves are represented mathematically as **y = A sin(ωt + φ)**, where A is the amplitude, ω is the angular frequency, and φ is the phase.
 
• The wave transitions smoothly between its maximum and minimum values, creating a symmetrical **S-shape** over one complete cycle.
 
• Sinusoidal waves are fundamental in physics, engineering, and mathematics due to their periodic and harmonic nature.
 
• Such waves are commonly used in **AC electrical signals**, sound waves, and other oscillatory systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Amplitude:**

 
 
• The maximum displacement of the wave from its mean position.
 
• Represents the strength or intensity of the wave.
 
 
 
• **Frequency:**
 
 
• The number of cycles completed per second, measured in Hertz (Hz).
 
• Higher frequency corresponds to faster oscillations.
 
 
 
• **Phase:**
 
 
• Defines the offset of the wave relative to a reference point.
 
• Critical for understanding wave interference and synchronization.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Sinusoidal Waves:**
 
 
• Used in alternating current (AC) electricity supply systems.
 
• Fundamental to sound wave analysis and signal processing.
 
• Critical in studying harmonic motion in physics and engineering.
 
 
 
• **Wave Equation:**
 
 
• A sinusoidal wave can be expressed as y = A sin(2πft + φ).
 
• This equation helps model real-world oscillatory phenomena.

questions.question: How many major ragas are there in Carnatic music?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**72**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In Carnatic music, there are **72 Melakarta ragas**, which are also called parent or fundamental ragas.
 
• The Melakarta system is a **comprehensive framework** for classifying all possible ragas based on specific scales.
 
• Each Melakarta raga consists of **seven swaras (notes)**: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Da, Ni, in ascending (Arohana) and descending (Avarohana) order.
 
• The 72 Melakarta ragas are divided into **12 chakras (groups)**, each containing six ragas.
 
• These Melakarta ragas serve as a foundation for deriving **Janya ragas**, which are more specific and commonly used in compositions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Melakarta Ragas:**

 
 
• Each Melakarta raga must have all seven swaras (notes) in both ascending (Arohana) and descending (Avarohana) scales.
 
• They strictly follow the rules of Carnatic music theory, such as having a fixed set of intervals between notes.
 
 
 
• **Chakras in Melakarta System:**
 
 
• The 72 Melakarta ragas are grouped into 12 chakras (sets), each named after a specific concept (e.g., Indu, Netra, Agni).
 
• Each chakra contains six Melakarta ragas, differentiated by variations in the Ri, Ga, Da, and Ni swaras.
 
 
 
• **Janya Ragas:**
 
 
• Janya ragas are derived from Melakarta ragas and may include fewer than seven swaras or employ irregular note patterns.
 
• They are more commonly used in Carnatic compositions and improvisations.
 
 
 
• **Swaras in Carnatic Music:**
 
 
• The seven basic swaras are: Shadja (Sa), Rishabha (Ri), Gandhara (Ga), Madhyama (Ma), Panchama (Pa), Dhaivata (Da), and Nishada (Ni).
 
• Each swara has variants (e.g., Shuddha, Chatushruti, Antara) that define the raga's scale.

questions.question: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is most prone to convoy effect, where a long-running process blocks shorter processes behind it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• FCFS is a non-preemptive scheduling algorithm where processes are executed in the order they arrive in the ready queue.
 
• This algorithm suffers from the **convoy effect**, where longer processes delay the execution of shorter ones, leading to inefficiency.
 
• Convoy effect occurs because FCFS does not consider the burst time of processes, causing an imbalance in CPU utilization.
 
• It is simple to implement but performs poorly in environments with a mix of long and short processes.
 
• In scenarios where a long process occupies the CPU, other processes must wait, leading to higher average waiting time and reduced throughput.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Convoy Effect**

 
 
• It is a situation in CPU scheduling where short processes get delayed due to a longer process occupying the CPU.
 
• It leads to increased waiting time, reduced throughput, and inefficient CPU utilization.
 
 
 
• **Other Scheduling Algorithms**
 
 
• **Priority Scheduling (non-preemptive):** Prioritizes processes based on a given priority, which can prevent convoy effect but may lead to starvation of lower-priority processes.
 
• **Shortest Job First (SJF):** Executes processes with the shortest burst time first, minimizing average waiting time and avoiding convoy effect in most cases.
 
• **Round Robin:** Uses a time quantum to ensure fair CPU allocation, effectively reducing the chances of convoy effect.
 
 
 
• **Preemptive vs Non-Preemptive Scheduling**
 
 
• **Preemptive Scheduling:** Allows the CPU to be taken away from a running process to execute a higher-priority or shorter process.
 
• **Non-Preemptive Scheduling:** Once a process starts execution, it runs to completion without interruption.
 
 
 
• **Metrics for Evaluating Scheduling Algorithms**
 
 
• **Turnaround Time:** Total time taken from process submission to completion.
 
• **Waiting Time:** Total time a process spends in the ready queue.
 
• **Throughput:** Number of processes completed per unit of time.
 
• **CPU Utilization:** Percentage of time the CPU remains active.

• **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**

 
 
• The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are a group of 572 islands located in the Bay of Bengal.
 
• They serve as India’s easternmost boundary and are of strategic importance for maritime trade and security.
 
• The islands act as a natural outpost for monitoring the **Malacca Strait**, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
 
 
 
• **Six Degree Channel**
 
 
• It is also known as the Great Channel and lies between the Great Nicobar Island and the Indonesian island of Sumatra.
 
• This channel is approximately 10 degrees north of the equator and is a crucial shipping route connecting the Indian Ocean to the Pacific Ocean.
 
 
 
• **Indian Naval Air Stations**
 
 
• Indian Naval Air Stations provide logistical and operational support for the Indian Navy’s air assets.
 
• Other key air stations include INS Hansa in Goa and INS Rajali in Tamil Nadu.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Importance of INS Baaz**
 
 
• The station enhances India’s ability to secure its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and monitor the **Indo-Pacific region**.
 
• It plays a key role in disaster relief operations, search and rescue missions, and maritime domain awareness.
